data.content_ref: inline:The mechanism section argues that the Popperian preference is justified because corroboration 'identifies the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, making it the most testable and thus the most informative candidate for further criticism,' and frames this as 'a methodological rule to maximize error detection.' The entire justification rests on structural properties of the theory (severity, testability, informativeness). The mechanism then concludes: 'It follows that the underlying structure was never relevant to the outcome at all.' This is a direct self-contradiction. If the structure (testability, severity of tests survived) is what licenses the preference, then structure is the very thing relevant to the outcome of the methodological choice. If instead 'the outcome' is read as future predictive success, the claim is still a non-sequitur: nothing in the preceding argument establishes that structure is 'never relevant' to future success—only that it provides no guarantee. 'Never relevant' is strictly stronger than 'not guaranteed' and is unsupported by the reasoning given. Either way, the conclusion does not follow from the premises and undercuts the argument's own grounding.
